Comparative Anti-Trypanosomal Activity of Azadirachta indica and Moringa oleifera against Trypanosoma congolense and T. evansi — Statistical Report

1 1. Aim, objectives and section map

The aim of this study is to comparatively evaluate the anti-trypanosomal activity of methanolic extracts of the leaves, stem bark, roots and seeds of Azadirachta indica and Moringa oleifera against Trypanosoma congolense and T. evansi (thesis §1.8.1). Each specific objective (§1.8.2) is addressed in a dedicated results section: extraction (i) in §5.1, phytochemical characterisation (ii) in §5.2, the in-vitro motility assay (iii) in §5.3, in-vivo infectivity monitoring (iv) in §5.4, and the comparative superiority assessment (v) in §5.5. The analysis protocol, diagnostic checks and limitations follow in §6–§7.

2 2. Data and experimental design

Source data are group means of n = 3 mice per group, parsed from Sheet 2 of the study workbook into tidy CSVs (analysis/data/, builder analysis/R/01_build_datasets.R). Within any plant × part × parasite block, each of the 7 groups (five concentrations plus two controls) is therefore n = 1 and supports description only. The analytical unit throughout is the block (N = 16; 8 per plant, 8 per parasite). Plant contrasts pair blocks by part × parasite (8 pairs); parasite contrasts pair by plant × part (8 pairs). Treatments appear as labelled in the source — Negative Control and Positive Control, whose identities and doses are not stated in Sheet 2 — so the Positive Control serves as an assay-validity reference only, not as a non-inferiority comparator.

3 3. Endpoints

Parasitaemia is recorded on the ordinal LEV scale (0–5). Because day-40 LEV proved degenerate (0 of 112 groups positive at day 40 — 68 zeros and 44 deaths — while positivity peaks near 30% around days 9–14), the primary parasitaemia endpoint is the AUC (death-censored trapezoidal sum over observed days, always reported alongside mortality), supported by peak LEV, clearance day and day-40 status. Motility (+/−) is summarised per group as time-to-immobilisation (TTI), proportion motile at t = 120 and mean proportion motile; the source key defines only + Active motility and − No motility (+- is undefined and was set to NA, 2 cells). Body weight and PCV use Δ = Post-Infection − Pre-Infection with literature-standard flags — anaemia at Post PCV < 35% or ≥ 25% relative drop (severe: < 30% or ≥ 40%; Noyes et al. 2009; Naessens et al. 2005; Gitonga et al. 2017) and weight-toxicity signal at ≥ 10% loss (severe: ≥ 20%, the standard humane-endpoint range). Raw LEV values above the 0–5 scale (42 cells: 41 decimals 5.01–5.3 plus one LEV = 6) were capped to 5 with pre-cap values preserved (lev_raw) and flagged. Missing in-vivo values are treated as animal death — an adopted convention, since Sheet 2 never states it — and are never imputed.

4 4. Statistical methods

Descriptive analysis is primary: trajectory plots per block, endpoint tables, and flag tabulations. Inference is entirely rank-based (LEV ordinal, N small): Friedman tests blocked by block for ordered dose trends with pooled Spearman ρ on log10(concentration) as the trend effect; paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (exact where the data permit, otherwise the continuity-corrected normal approximation — see §6) for dose-vs-control and for plant/parasite contrasts, each with the matched-pairs rank-biserial effect size (Cliff’s delta family; |r| ≥ 0.11/0.28/0.43 small/medium/large per Vargha & Delaney 2000) and the Hodges–Lehmann median difference with 95% CI. The dose-vs-control Wilcoxons are the formal post-hoc family following each omnibus trend test, Holm-adjusted per parasite; plant and parasite contrasts address independent questions and are not corrected across questions. Per-block trend tests at n = 1 have no power and pooled trend tests would break independence, so only the blocked Friedman is reported as inference. Significance is set at p < 0.05 with p-values supplementary to effect sizes. All computation is in analysis/R/02_analysis.R (statistics only, no machine learning).

5 5.1. Objective i — methanolic extraction

Objective i (extraction of leaves, stem bark, roots and seeds of both plants under standard phytochemical protocols) is a laboratory procedure with no statistical component: no yields or replicates are recorded in the available data, so there is nothing to estimate or test. It is reported here only to keep the objective map complete; efficacy inference begins with the characterised extracts in §5.2–§5.5.

6 5.2. Objective ii — phytochemical contents

Screening detected all 12 assayed compound classes across the design, with richness concentrated in leaves and seeds (Table 1). M. oleifera leaves carry the broadest profile (9 of 12 classes present) while stem bark in both plants is the sparsest fraction; no compound is unique to a single plant part in a way that alone explains efficacy. Because only eight plant × part combinations exist, these data support description only: the presence matrix (Figure 1) is the result, and any compound–efficacy association is an exploratory overlay tabulated without inference in phytochemical_efficacy_overlay.csv.

7 5.3. Objective iii — in-vitro motility dose response

Motility collapses with both time and concentration in every block (Figure 2): Negative Controls remain motile through 120 minutes while 100 mg/ml immobilises parasites within 15–30 minutes in most blocks, and the recovered Positive Control rows show the expected rapid kill (+ at t = 0, immobile thereafter). Group-level summaries (TTI, t120, mean proportion motile; endpoints_motility.csv) confirm the pattern numerically — TTI is derivable for 82 of 112 groups, the remainder being groups that never immobilise (chiefly Negative Controls). The blocked dose–response test is highly significant for both parasites (Table 2: T. congolense Friedman Q = 27.75, p < 0.001, pooled ρ = −0.70; T. evansi Q = 30.32, p < 0.001, ρ = −0.88), and mean AUC-equivalent motility falls monotonically with log-concentration. Post-hoc dose-vs-control contrasts (Table 3) show large, consistent effects at the top doses (rank-biserial −1; HL reduction ≈ −0.83 for congolense 100 mg/ml and −0.89 for evansi 100 mg/ml) that sit just above the Holm-adjusted threshold (Holm 0.065 and 0.052) — strong but, at N = 8 blocks, formally inconclusive after multiplicity control. Lower doses are indistinguishable from the control.

8 5.4. Objective iv — in-vivo infectivity

8.1 Parasitaemia

LEV trajectories rise from day 1, peak around days 9–14 and resolve toward zero by day 40 in survivors (Figure 4); mortality (44 of 112 groups with at least one dead-animal day, first deaths days 9–37) accompanies the decline, which is why AUC rather than day-40 LEV carries the inference. Cumulative burden falls monotonically with concentration (Figure 3), significantly for T. evansi (Table 4: Friedman Q = 14.51, p = 0.006, pooled ρ = −0.51) and suggestively for T. congolense (Q = 8.52, p = 0.074, ρ = −0.42). Post-hoc contrasts (Table 5) confirm the gradient for T. evansi: 100, 10 and 0.5 mg/ml each beat the Negative Control in all eight blocks (W = 0, exact p = 0.008, Holm 0.039; HL ≈ −50/−50/−44 AUC-days), while 0.01 and 0.005 mg/ml do not survive correction (Holm 0.078). For T. congolense only 100 mg/ml is suggestive (p = 0.014, Holm 0.071) and no dose is significant after correction. No parasite-level difference in AUC was found (paired p = 0.46; Table 6).

8.2 Body weight and PCV

Weight and PCV deltas centre near zero with wide scatter (Figure 5, Figure 6); neither plant nor parasite contrasts approach significance (Table 6: weight plant p = 0.31, parasite p = 0.15; PCV plant p = 0.74, parasite p = 0.95). Toxicity and anaemia flags (endpoints_weight.csv, endpoints_pcv.csv) are therefore the substantive read-out: they identify the groups paying a physiological price for infection regardless of treatment, consistent with efficacy that is parasitological rather than confounded by differential toxicity.

9 5.5. Objective v — comparative superiority

There is no evidence that either plant is superior. Block-mean AUC pairs scatter on both sides of identity (Figure 7): paired W = 14, exact p = 1.0, HL ≈ 0.3 AUC-days with 95% CI (−14.7, +20.5), rank-biserial −0.14 (Table 7). The motility cross-check agrees (paired p = 0.15, HL 0.11). With only eight pairs the interval spans effects in both directions, so the data cannot support a superiority claim for either agent; the correct conclusion is the null, stated with its confidence interval rather than as a bare p-value.

10 6. Diagnostics, sensitivity and refits

Three diagnostics were run and each changed or confirmed the analysis. First, rank-test validity: several contrasts contain tied absolute differences (all five T. congolense dose contrasts; most motility contrasts, whose endpoint averages nine binary points) or dropped zero differences (plant superiority: one of eight pairs). Because R’s exact Wilcoxon distribution is invalid with tied ranks, every contrast now records n_nonzero, n_ties and p_method, using the exact p-value only when neither occurs and the continuity-corrected normal approximation otherwise — this refit left all conclusions unchanged (e.g. congolense 100 mg/ml: asymptotic p = 0.014, Holm 0.071). Second, paired-difference symmetry, the remaining signed-rank assumption, was inspected visually (Figure 8): the evansi differences sit entirely below zero (a location shift, unproblematic for the test), while the superiority differences spread symmetrically around zero, matching its null result. Third, leave-one-block-out sensitivity (Table 8) shows every headline claim is stable — no single block flips any conclusion (evansi top doses: LOO p = 0.016 throughout; superiority null: LOO p 0.53–1.0). Completeness was verified structurally (4480/336/336/1008/96 rows with 4 part levels enforced at build).

11 7. Limitations

Each CSV row is a mean of n = 3 mice, so no within-group variance survives and all inference rests on N = 16 blocks (8 per contrast) — power is low, intervals are wide, and descriptive patterns carry the weight. Control identities and doses are unknown in the source, so the Positive Control is a validity reference, not a comparator. Death-censored AUC favours early-death groups numerically, hence every AUC is read alongside mortality. NA = death is an adopted convention worth confirming against the animal records. All results are exploratory, not confirmatory.
